reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: NIST defines the recovery point objective (RPO) as the point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage. Here backups complete at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00, each is assumed to be restorable, and no other copy of the data exists.

Independent check: for periodic backups the worst-case loss equals the backup interval plus any delay before a backup becomes usable. With a 6-hour interval and no delay the bound is 6 hours, consistent with the 11:59 example.

Misconception to reject: 'the RPO is how quickly we restore.' Restore speed is governed by the RTO; the RPO concerns how old the recovered data may be. A fast restore of a 6-hour-old backup still misses a 1-hour RPO.
Change one factor: take snapshots every 30 minutes. The worst-case loss falls to 30 minutes, within the 1-hour RPO, provided each snapshot is complete and restorable.

Source and limits: the RPO definition follows NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-34r1. A backup that fails a restore test provides no recovery point, so schedule restore tests as well as backups.

reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic dependency graph: activation takes 10 minutes, then database restore takes 40 and application preparation takes 25 in parallel, followed by 10 minutes of joint validation. All durations start after their prerequisites finish.
Total recovery is 10 + max(40,25) + 10 = 60 minutes. The database branch is on the critical path.

These gains assume unconstrained parallel resources and unchanged correctness checks. Optimize the measured critical path, not the visually longest task list or a task that merely seems easy to accelerate.
